text.p: Britain's new Labour government on Wednesday announced a "national crusade" to combat youth unemployment and said it would be very tough with young people who refused the offer of a job or training.

Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown held a breakfast meeting with executives from 50 top companies to explain the three billion pound ($5 billion) "welfare-to-work" programme that will form the centrepiece of his first budget next week.

Under the programme, employers will receive 60 pounds a week for six months for every unemployed person under 25 to whom they give a job. The subsidy is 75 pounds for job offers to someone out of work for more than two years.
In a series of early morning radio and television interviews, Brown said he aimed to prevent the emergence in Britain of an "underclass" of unemployable and disaffected young people.
"I am determined that we are not going to let the situation in our country deteriorate further," he said.

"What we are launching today is, in effect, a national crusade to persuade employers as well as voluntary organisations and environmental organisations...that we should all be involved in tackling this serious social problem."

The welfare to work programme will be financed by a one-off "windfall tax" on the profits made by utility companies privatised by the previous Conservative government. It is intended to create work for 250,000 young people.
Brown said Britain had half a million unemployed young people. Youth unemployment was higher than in Germany and reached 30 percent of the young population in some inner-city areas.

The programme would offer young people four options -- a job, a training place, work on an environmental taskforce or a placement with a voluntary organisation. But those who chose simply to do nothing would be penalised.
"There is no fifth option. They will lose some of their benefit if they refuse to take up a place," Brown said.

"Where government and society provide opportunities, then for young people, obligations do go with that. And therefore yes, we are prepared to be very tough in ensuring that nobody who is given the offer of this new opportunity to get work can turn it down without facing consequences."
The Chancellor noted that were skill shortages in many sectors of industry throughout Britain and he was confident the training opportunities would lead to real jobs.
Even though the windfall tax was a one-off levy, it would finance the programme for five years.
"We are not creating a programme that will last for six months and then run out of money. We have costed it over a five-year parliament," Brown said.

"We are putting money into this programme -- three billion pounds of government money -- so that we can break this vicious cycle of poverty, unemployment, lack of skills and therefore unemployability." ($ = 0.599 British Pounds)
